Time to Play B-Sides: Penny Lane/Strawberry Fields Forever

This is a real treat, one of the greatest Double A-Side Singles of all time. But more than being two great songs, Penny Lane and Strawberry Fields showed the different sides of the respective songwriters, and also signaled the start of a growing rift in a songwriting partnership that would ultimately breakup the Beatles.

By the end of 1966, the Beatles were exhausted from touring. An Asian swing that saw them get a lot of guff in Japan and almost killed in the Philippines, as well as an American tour that was underwhelming had left John, Paul, George and Ringo fed up with the road. In addition, the band became interested in what they could create in a recording studio, as shown by the experimental Tomorrow Never Knows and the big band horns of Got to Get You Into My Life from Revolver. The Beatles wanted more of that, and the inability to re-create the sound on the road due to limitations at the time (Jim Marshall was just getting his revolutionary Marshall Stack amps onto the market) and screaming fans made them decide to become a studio group.

The first two products of this decision came out on January 17, 1967, and they changed rock music. Both songs embrace psychedelia, but are quite different and reflect their respective songwriter's personalities.

Interestingly, both songs are set in Liverpool, the hometown of the Beatles. But where Penny Lane is all brightness and sunshine, Strawberry Fields is darker and more downbeat. This is no accident, as the songs are about the songwriters' childhoods.

Although credited to Lennon-McCartney, Penny Lane is all Macca. Paul grew up in a middle class part of Liverpool in a happy home. His parents had a happy marriage and both had good jobs. Sadly, that changed when Paul's mom died from complications brought on by breast cancer, but by then he was 14 and was mature enough to handle some of the pain. Penny Lane reflects Paul's happy childhood. It is set downtown and Paul sings brightly about the sights and sounds of his little slice of the world. The piccolo trumpet solo by David Mason reflects with its cheerful fanfare.

From all indications, John Lennon had a miserable childhood. His dad was in the merchant marines and away from home for long stretches, while his mom Julia coped with what would now be diagnosed as mental health issues. It came to a head when his dad returned from the war with the intent of taking John permanently away to New Zealand, demanding this five year old boy choose between mom and dad. Yes, it was that bad. He ended up choosing mom and didn't see his dad for 20 years. Meanwhile, his mom couldn't raise John and left him in the care of his aunt Mimi and her husband. Psychologists have surmised that this is why John always sought out relationships with older women. Who knows? But from great pain comes great art, and such is the case with Strawberry Fields.

Strawberry Fields is a very dark song. It has modalities and tonalities taken from Eastern music, and features odd instruments such as the guiro and the swarmandal. In addition, John, Paul and George add eerie Mellotron parts, with horn and string sections playing discordant fills. Reverse taping (used in songs like Rain and Tomorrow Never Knows to add psychedelic color) only increases the discomfort in the track. The title itself references a Salvation Army home for orphans named Strawberry Field where John played as a little boy. His choice of singing Strawberry Fields Forever reflects his yearning for a lost childhood, a happy time he never had, as well as feeling like an orphan with a physically distant father and an emotionally distant mother.

While the single was a hit for both songs, it showed that Lennon and McCartney weren't collaborating like they had been previously. Sure, you can tell which song sprang from an idea of John or Paul, but the other would often get involved in the songwriting process, with Paul polishing John's songs to make his ideas more commercially appealing, and John adding an edge to some of Paul's more pop musical ideas. By the end, John would be sneering about Paul's grandma songs and Paul lamenting that many of John's contributions were unlistenable.

#MSNews | The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), through the Philippine Consulate in Hong Kong, confirms that one OFW is missing while one is confined to the ICU of a local hospital following the Level 5 fire that engulfed a residential complex in Tai Po, New Territories.

It also reported that a total of 23 Filipino domestic workers required welfare assistance. | via Katrina Manubay

📷 Agence France Presse

For more news updates, visit https://t.co/rmQCnNSOvI.
